n: News spread quickly: Gentiles — non-Jews — had accepted the gospel at Cornelius’s house. For a church that was entirely Jewish so far, this was startling and needed explaining.

f.w: the Gentiles had also received the word of God

n: Back in Jerusalem, some Jewish believers who insisted on the law of Moses challenged Peter. “They of the circumcision” means Jewish Christians who felt Gentile converts must first become Jews.

f.w: they that were of the circumcision
f.g: Jewish Christians who held that circumcision and the law of Moses were still required.

n: Their complaint was not mainly about baptism but about table fellowship. Strict Jews avoided eating with Gentiles, whose food and homes were considered ritually unclean.
Instead of arguing, Peter simply told the story step by step. Letting the facts speak was the wisest way to show that God, not Peter, had opened this door.

f.g: In sequence, from start to finish.

n: Peter retells his vision in Joppa, the seaport where he had been staying. A great sheet came down from heaven, lowered by its four corners.

f.g: Modern Jaffa, the port next to today’s Tel Aviv.

f.w: in a trance I saw a vision

n: The sheet held every kind of animal, including ones the law of Moses forbade Israelites to eat. Peter looked closely, and the sight would have shocked any faithful Jew.
A voice commanded Peter to kill and eat. The command seemed to contradict everything he had kept his whole life.
Peter protested that he had never eaten anything forbidden. “Common” here means ordinary or profane — not set apart as clean under the law.

f.g: “Common” = ritually ordinary, unfit for a holy people; “unclean” = forbidden by the law.

n: The heart of the vision: what God has made clean, Peter must not call unclean. The lesson went beyond food — it was about people, as Peter came to understand.

f.w: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common

n: The vision repeated three times, underlining its importance. Then everything was taken back up to heaven.
Right at that moment, messengers from Cornelius arrived. The timing showed Peter that the vision and the visitors belonged together.

f.g: Roman capital of Judea on the Mediterranean coast, about 30 miles north of Joppa.

n: The Spirit told Peter to go without hesitating. He wisely brought six Jewish brethren as witnesses — and they are now present in Jerusalem to confirm his account.
Cornelius had also been visited by an angel, who told him to send for Peter. God had been preparing both men at the same time.

f.w: he had seen an angel in his house

n: The angel promised that Peter’s message would bring salvation to Cornelius and his whole household. The gospel was meant for families.

f.w: thou and all thy house shall be saved

n: Before Peter had even finished, the Holy Ghost came upon these Gentiles just as it had on the apostles at Pentecost. God himself had given the sign of acceptance.

f.w: as on us at the beginning

n: Peter remembered Jesus’ promise that his disciples would be baptized with the Holy Ghost. Seeing it happen to Gentiles proved they were included.

f.w: ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost

n: Peter’s conclusion: if God gave them the same gift he gave us, who was I to stand in God’s way? Refusing them baptism would have meant resisting God.

f.w: what was I, that I could withstand God?

n: The critics were satisfied and praised God. A major turning point: the Church now officially recognized that repentance and eternal life were open to the Gentiles too.

f.g: Repentance that leads to eternal life.

n: Luke now picks up another thread. Believers who fled Jerusalem after Stephen’s death carried the gospel north — but at first only to fellow Jews.

f.w: the persecution that arose about Stephen

f.g: Phoenicia — the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, in modern Lebanon.

n: Some Jewish believers from Cyprus and North Africa took a bold step in Antioch: they taught Greek-speaking Gentiles too. “Grecians” here likely means Greeks rather than Greek-speaking Jews.

f.g: Antioch in Syria, the third-largest city of the Roman Empire.
A city in North Africa, in modern Libya.

n: God blessed their work, and many people turned to the Lord. Antioch would become the home base for the Church’s mission to the Gentiles.

f.g: A biblical idiom for God’s power and help.

n: The Jerusalem leaders sent Barnabas to check on this new growth. He was a trusted, generous disciple and himself from Cyprus.
Barnabas didn’t come to criticize — he saw God’s grace at work and rejoiced. He urged the new converts to hold to the Lord with full determination.
Luke praises Barnabas as a good man, full of the Spirit and faith. Under such leadership, still more people joined the Church.
Barnabas went to Tarsus, Paul’s hometown, to look for Saul. He remembered this converted persecutor and saw the work he could do.
Barnabas and Saul taught in Antioch for a full year. There the followers of Jesus were first called “Christians” — people belonging to Christ.

f.g: Greek Christianoi — “partisans of Christ”; probably a nickname given by outsiders.

n: Prophets — inspired teachers who could foretell events — came from Jerusalem. The gift of prophecy was active in the early Church.
Agabus foretold a severe famine across the Roman world. It happened under Emperor Claudius (AD 41–54), when historians record several food shortages.
The Antioch saints each gave what they could to help the believers in Judea. A Gentile-founded church caring for Jewish saints showed their unity in Christ.

f.w: every man according to his ability

n: They sent the relief to the Jerusalem elders through Barnabas and Saul. This is the first mention of elders as leaders in the Church.

f.g: Local leaders of the Church; an office of the priesthood.
